Fact.Name: Parental Situation Options
Fact.Description: Options for parental situation
The options for who has taken a written declaration to not claim a child, sometimes via Form 8332

Fact.Name: Flow variable for special rule benefit split
Fact.Description:
Whether or not to show the benefit split screens for the dependent. We have to test for the special benefit split if the person is subject to custody.
Custody ends when the child is emancipated under the law of the state where the child lives, and the age at which that happens is not 18 in every state. The special rule reaches a child only while the child is in a parent's custody for more than half of the tax year, so an emancipation on or before July 2 closes the split (2025 Publication 504 Example 5) while one after July 2 leaves the first half of the year, and the split, intact (Example 6).
../ageOfMajorityForCustodyTest is used ONLY to decide WHEN the emancipation question has to be asked. A dependent who has not reached that age by the close of the tax year opens the split without being asked at all, the same as it always has; this arm needs no state answer for a dependent under the universal floor of 18, since no state sets an age of majority below that. A dependent who has reached the age must answer ../writableChildEmancipatedUnderStateLaw, and the answer decides, not the age: an emancipated dependent below that age is taken out of the split exactly like one above it, and an unanswered state or an unanswered emancipation question, once the question must be asked, leaves this whole fact Incomplete rather than assuming an age of majority of 18. A permanently and totally disabled dependent has no age ceiling at all. An emancipation answered Yes with a date on or before the custody midyear (July 2) closes the split on every arm, whatever the dependent's age or disability, because an emancipated child is treated as not living with either parent; a Yes with no date yet leaves this fact Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Child emancipated under state law
Fact.Description:
SCREEN. Question: "Was {name} emancipated under your state's law during 2025?" Help text: a child who is emancipated under state law is treated as not living with either parent, so the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents can stop applying. The law that counts is the state where the CHILD lives, which for a noncustodial parent is often not the filer's own state. Answer Yes even if the emancipation happened before 2025 too: once a child is emancipated the child stays emancipated, and this question is really asking about the child's status through the end of the tax year, not only about an event that happened during it. (This help-text widening past the project owner's literal "during 2025" wording is a deliberate fix for a filer who would otherwise answer No because the emancipation happened in an earlier year, even though the child has, in fact, stayed emancipated ever since.)
Asked only when ../ageOfMajorityForCustodyTest has been reached by the close of the tax year (../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit's own Description explains why): a younger dependent already opens the benefit split and is never asked. Unanswered when it must be asked, this fact and everything it feeds resolve Incomplete, never defaulted to either answer: an unanswered custody question holds the return rather than guessing an age of majority of 18 for it.
What the answer feeds: ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit directly. A No keeps the child in custody. A Yes moves to ../writableChildEmancipationDate, because a child emancipated after the midyear point of the tax year was still in custody for more than half of it.

Fact.Name: Date the child was emancipated under state law
Fact.Description: SCREEN. Question: "On what date was {name} emancipated under state law?" Help text: enter the date {name} became emancipated, even if it was before 2025. Asked when: ../writableChildEmancipatedUnderStateLaw is Yes. Unanswered posture: neither ../childEmancipationDateAfterCustodyMidyear nor ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit resolves; both stay Incomplete until the date is entered, because a bare Yes with no date does not say whether the child was still in custody for more than half of the tax year. Validation: Day, no later than 2025-12-31 (a date after this tax year cannot describe an event within it). What the answer feeds: ../childEmancipationDateAfterCustodyMidyear, which compares the date to July 2, 2025, the same midyear point this module uses elsewhere for the more-than-half-the-year custody test.

Fact.Name: The emancipation date is after the tax year's custody midyear point
Fact.Description: Whether the entered emancipation date falls after July 2, 2025 - the point this module treats as more than half of a 365-day tax year (183 of 365 days have run by the end of July 2, one more than half of 365). An emancipation on or before that date means the child was not in a parent's custody for more than half the year (2025 Publication 504 Example 5); one after that date leaves the custody condition met even though the child is emancipated before the year ends (Example 6, where an August 1 emancipation still leaves the custodial parent with the greater number of nights for the year). INCOMPLETE while the date is unanswered: a Yes with no date does not yet say which half of the year is affected. An entered date after 2025-12-31 cannot describe an event inside the tax year, so it is read the conservative way, as not after the midyear point, rather than trusted (the Writable's Limit is JVM-validation only and does not fire on the JS default engine).

Fact.Name: States, territories and outside the United States, for a child's residence
Fact.Description: The vocabulary of ../writableChildResidenceJurisdiction on each dependent: the 50 states and the District of Columbia (the same codes as constants:/scopedStateOptions), then Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, then outsideUnitedStates. Puerto Rico is listed because its age of majority is one of the four that differ from 18; the other territories and outsideUnitedStates keep the default age of 18 in /familyAndHousehold/*/ageOfMajorityForCustodyTest.

Fact.Name: State or territory where the child lived on July 2
Fact.Description:
In which state or U.S. territory does the dependent live? Choose outsideUnitedStates if the child lives outside the United States.
Asked only for a dependent who has reached ../ageOfMajorityForCustodyTest by the close of the tax year and is not permanently and totally disabled: a younger child already opens the benefit split through ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit without needing this answer. The answer is the CHILD's state, not the filer's: custody ends when the child is emancipated under the law of the state where the child lives, and for a noncustodial parent that state is often not the one in /filerResidenceAndIncomeState.
Unanswered, when it must be asked, ../ageOfMajorityForCustodyTest and everything it feeds are Incomplete: the state is not knowable without an answer, so this fact is never defaulted to an age of majority of 18.

Fact.Name: Age of majority that ends custody for the benefit split
Fact.Description:
The age at which the dependent stops being in a parent's custody for the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents: 19 when ../writableChildResidenceJurisdiction is Alabama or Nebraska, 21 when it is Mississippi or Puerto Rico, and 18 for every other answered state. ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit reads this fact ONLY to decide WHEN a dependent has to answer ../writableChildEmancipatedUnderStateLaw: a dependent younger than this age by the close of the tax year opens the benefit split without being asked; the answer decides for everyone else, not this age.
UNANSWERED, this fact is INCOMPLETE, not 18: the state is not knowable without an answer, and a dependent old enough for the question to matter must not be defaulted into or out of the split by an assumed age of majority. ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit is written so that an unanswered state never affects a dependent below the universal floor of 18, which needs no state to resolve.
The IRS text does not tabulate these ages. It says a child emancipated under state law is treated as not living with either parent, and that the law of the state where the child lives governs. The four ages that differ from 18 are taken from those states' own statutes, which are not among the vendored sources.
The relationship to the person is a parental one for use in the special benefit split
The relationship to the person is not a parental one for use in the special benefit split

Fact.Name: Has other legal parent
Fact.Description: Does the dependent have another legal parent apart from the taxpayer and spouse?

Fact.Name: Written declaration not to claim was signed
Fact.Description: Has any of the dependent's parents signed a written declaration not to claim them?
Is one of the parents not claiming the child?

Fact.Name: The date the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect
Fact.Description: SCREEN. Question: "When did the divorce decree, separate maintenance decree or written separation agreement covering {name} go into effect?" Help text: the date matters because the law treats three vintages differently. An instrument executed before January 1, 1985 can give the claim to the noncustodial parent on its own terms. One that went into effect after 1984 and before 2009 can stand in for Form 8332 if it says the right things. One that went into effect after 2008 cannot: the custodial parent has to sign Form 8332 or a similar statement. Enter the date the decree or agreement took effect, not the date it was last amended; the date it was signed is asked separately, in ../writableDivorceOrSeparationInstrumentExecutionDate, because the pre-1985 test is on the signing date and the later two are on the effective date. Asked when: this person's benefit-split questions are being asked and the taxpayer answered ../parentalSituation as divorced or separated. Unanswered posture: no decree route is available, so both route facts resolve Complete FALSE and the return falls back on the written declaration exactly as it does today. That is the correct refusal for a condition of allowance: a claim the graph cannot substantiate is not granted. Validation: Day, no later than 2025-12-31 (an instrument that takes effect after this tax year cannot apply to it). The Limit is JVM-validation-only, so ../divorceOrSeparationInstrumentEffectiveDateAdmissible is the value-level guard the two route facts read. What the answer feeds: ../instrumentEffectiveAfter1984AndBefore2009 (the decree-pages route), and ../instrumentExecutedBefore1985 (the IRC 152(e)(3) route) only while ../writableDivorceOrSeparationInstrumentExecutionDate is unanswered; an instrument after 2008 satisfies neither, which IS the printed bar.

Fact.Name: The date the divorce decree or separation agreement was signed
Fact.Description: SCREEN. Question: "When was the divorce decree, separate maintenance decree or written separation agreement covering {name} signed?" Help text: a decree or agreement signed before January 1, 1985 can give the claim to the noncustodial parent on its own terms, even if it took effect later. Enter the date it was signed (for a court decree, the date the court entered it), not the date it took effect and not the date it was last amended. Asked when: ../writableDivorceOrSeparationInstrumentEffectiveDate is answered. Unanswered posture: ../instrumentExecutedBefore1985 reads the effective date in its place, which is how every return that does not answer this question resolved before it was added. Answered, this date alone decides the pre-1985 test, in both directions: an instrument signed in 1984 that took effect in 1985 qualifies, and one signed in 1985 with an effective date earlier than its signing does not. Validation: Day, no later than 2025-12-31. What the answer feeds: ../instrumentExecutedBefore1985 only; the two later vintages are banded on the effective date, which is how the instructions print them.

Fact.Name: The instrument's effective date is answered and inside the admissible band
Fact.Description: Whether the entered effective date is complete and no later than the tax year's own last day. The Writable's Limit type="Max" enforces the same bound only at JVM validation time (a Limit on a Writable fires as a validation Error, never at resolution), and the JS path is the default engine, so an out-of-bound date is not refused there at all. This derived fact is the value-level guard both route facts route through, in exactly the shape familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/dateOfBirthAdmissible takes for the dependent's date of birth. Complete-safe FALSE while the date is unanswered, which is what keeps every return with no decree question answered byte-identical.

Fact.Name: The instrument was executed before January 1, 1985
Fact.Description:
IRC 152(e)(3)(B)(i), the first of the three tests a "qualified pre-1985 instrument" has to meet: it must be "executed before January 1, 1985". STRICTLY BEFORE, so an instrument dated 1984-12-31 qualifies and one dated 1985-01-01 does not. Complete-safe FALSE while the date is unanswered or inadmissible.
THE TEST IS ON THE SIGNING DATE. The statute says "executed", so when ../writableDivorceOrSeparationInstrumentExecutionDate is answered it alone decides: an instrument signed in 1984 that took effect in 1985 qualifies (split-152e3-instrument-executed-1984-effective-1985-pre1985-route-met), and one signed in 1985 with an earlier effective date does not (split-152e3-instrument-effective-1984-executed-1985-not-qualified). While the signing date is unanswered the effective date stands in for it, which is the reading every earlier return resolved under.

Fact.Name: The pre-1985 instrument gives the claim to the noncustodial parent and was never modified to take it back
Fact.Description:
SCREEN. Question: "Does that decree or agreement say the other parent can claim {name} as a dependent, and has it never been changed since 1984 to say they cannot?" Help text: for a decree or agreement that took effect before 1985, the document itself can give the claim to the parent the child does not live with, with no Form 8332 needed. Answer Yes only if all of this is true: the decree or agreement applies to 2025, it says the noncustodial parent can claim the child as a dependent, and it was not changed on or after January 1, 1985 in a change that says this rule no longer applies. Asked when: this person's benefit-split questions are being asked and ../writableDivorceOrSeparationInstrumentEffectiveDate is before 1985-01-01. Unanswered posture: Complete FALSE through ../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet, so the route is not taken and the return falls back on the written declaration. A CONDITION OF ALLOWANCE reads silence as "not established" - the graph does not grant a claim it cannot substantiate - which is also why an Incomplete is wrong here: an unanswered question about a route the filer may not even be on must not stop the return. Validation: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, answer required to leave the screen. What the answer feeds: ../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet, one of three conjuncts.
THIS IS THREE STATUTORY TESTS IN ONE QUESTION, and they are kept together because they are three properties of one document that only the filer can read: IRC 152(e)(3)(A)(i) (the instrument "provides that the noncustodial parent shall be entitled to any deduction allowable under section 151 for such child"), 152(e)(3)(B)(ii) (it contained that provision on 1985-01-01) and 152(e)(3)(B)(iii) (it "is not modified on or after such date in a modification which expressly provides that this paragraph shall not apply"). Splitting them into three screens would ask the filer to parse the statute rather than read their decree.

Fact.Name: Support the noncustodial parent provided for this child during the year, for the section 152(e)(3) $600 test
Fact.Description: SCREEN. Question: "How much did the parent {name} does not live with provide for {name}'s support during 2025?" Help text: the pre-1985 decree route has a support floor the Form 8332 route does not: the noncustodial parent has to provide at least $600 for the child's support during the year. Count everything that parent spent on the child's support; under a pre-1985 agreement, all child support payments actually received from the noncustodial parent count as used for the child's support even if they were spent on something else. Asked when: ../instrumentExecutedBefore1985 is true and ../writableQualifiedPre1985InstrumentGivesClaimToNoncustodialParent is Yes. Unanswered posture: $0 through ../pre1985InstrumentSupportTestMet, which fails the $600 test and refuses the route. That is the taxpayer-adverse direction and the right one for a condition of allowance. Validation: Dollar, Min $0, ONE amount per person. What the answer feeds: ../pre1985InstrumentSupportTestMet.

Fact.Name: The section 152(e)(3)(A)(ii) $600 support floor is met
Fact.Description: IRC 152(e)(3)(A)(ii): the noncustodial parent "provides at least $600 for the support of such child during such calendar year". AT LEAST, so $600 exactly passes and $599 fails. The amount reads $0 while unanswered, so an unasked question fails the floor and refuses the route rather than granting it. THIS FLOOR IS ON THE PRE-1985 LEG ONLY: neither the Form 8332 route (IRC 152(e)(2)) nor the post-1984/pre-2009 decree route carries it, and the instructions for the decree-pages route say the opposite, that the claim must be "without regard to any condition, such as payment of support".

Fact.Name: Section 152(e)(1) is satisfied through paragraph (3), the qualified pre-1985 instrument
Fact.Description:
IRC 152(e)(1) is met when "the requirements described in paragraph (2) OR (3)" are met. Paragraph (2) is the written declaration this module already models through ../whichParentNotClaiming. THIS FACT IS PARAGRAPH (3): all three of its tests at once - the instrument was executed before 1985 (../instrumentExecutedBefore1985), it gives the claim to the noncustodial parent and was never modified to take it back (../writableQualifiedPre1985InstrumentGivesClaimToNoncustodialParent), and the $600 support floor is met (../pre1985InstrumentSupportTestMet).
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE, every conjunct. A return that never opens the decree questions is byte-identical to what it is today, and a return that opens them and leaves one unanswered is REFUSED the route rather than left Incomplete: this is a condition of allowance, and a claim the graph cannot substantiate is not granted. That posture is also what protects the corpus - ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc is read under an All(IsComplete(x), x) gate at familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation and /eligibleCtc, so an Incomplete arm here would put every dependent's claim Incomplete across the whole corpus.
WHERE IT GOES, four places, all in this module: ../parentalSomeParentNotClaiming (so ../eligibleForBenefitSplit opens on the parental path), the noncustodial arm of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc, the custodial arm of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc (the custodial parent who lost the dependency claim under the decree keeps head of household, the earned income credit and the child and dependent care credit - the "both" direction), and ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached, which must NOT refuse this population: Form 8332 page 2 item 3b states this route with no attachment at all, and the Form 1040 instruction's condition 4 is "Either of the following applies", 4a being Form 8332 and 4b being this instrument.
THE POPULATION IS NARROW BUT NOT EMPTY. An unmodified pre-1985 instrument implies a marriage that predates 1985, so most named children are past dependent age by 2025 - but a permanently and totally disabled qualifying child has no age ceiling (familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/permanentTotalDisability), and IRC 152(e)(3)(B)(iii) keeps an unmodified instrument live indefinitely.

Fact.Name: The decree or agreement went into effect after 1984 and before 2009
Fact.Description: The middle of the three vintages the law bands ../writableDivorceOrSeparationInstrumentEffectiveDate into: "If the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect after 1984 and before 2009, the noncustodial parent may be able to include certain pages from the decree or agreement instead of Form 8332." Read as 1985-01-01 through 2008-12-31 inclusive, which is what "after 1984 and before 2009" means on a calendar-year boundary. Both edges are on the EFFECTIVE date, as printed; the pre-1985 test is on the signing date, so an instrument signed in 1984 that took effect in 1985 can meet both, and either route may then be used. THE UPPER EDGE IS THE PRINTED BAR, not a modelling choice: "Post-2008 decree or agreement. If the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect after 2008, the noncustodial parent can't include pages from the decree or agreement instead of Form 8332." A post-2008 instrument therefore satisfies neither this fact nor ../instrumentExecutedBefore1985, and the filer is left on the Form 8332 route, which is the correct answer. Complete-safe FALSE while the date is unanswered or inadmissible.

Fact.Name: The post-1984 and pre-2009 decree states all three things the instruction requires
Fact.Description:
SCREEN. Question: "Does that decree or agreement say all three of these things about {name}?" with the three printed statements listed as they are printed: (1) the other parent can claim {name} as a dependent without regard to any condition, such as payment of support; (2) you will not claim {name} as a dependent; (3) the years for which the claim is released. Help text: for a decree or agreement that went into effect after 1984 and before 2009, the pages of the decree can stand in for Form 8332 - but only if the decree says all three of these things. You have to include the cover page (with the other parent's Social Security number on it), the pages carrying the three statements, and the signature page with the other parent's signature and the date of the agreement, and you have to include them even if you filed them with a return in an earlier year. Asked when: ../instrumentEffectiveAfter1984AndBefore2009 is true. Unanswered posture: Complete FALSE through ../post1984Pre2009DecreeRouteMet, so the route is not taken and the return falls back on Form 8332. A CONDITION OF ALLOWANCE reads silence as "not established". Validation: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, answer required to leave the screen. What the answer feeds: ../post1984Pre2009DecreeRouteMet.
THE WORDING OF THE QUESTION IS FROM THE OTHER PARENT'S SIDE OR THE FILER'S, depending on who is answering, and the application substitutes accordingly: ../tpIsCustodialParent says which side of the decree this filer is on, and the three statements are the same statements either way.
THE THREE ARE ONE QUESTION for the same reason the pre-1985 attestation is: they are three properties of one document that only the filer can read, and asking them separately would invite a Yes on two of three that the instruction does not allow. NO SUPPORT FLOOR ON THIS ROUTE, deliberately - statement (1) is the opposite, the claim must be unconditional "such as payment of support"; the $600 floor belongs to the pre-1985 leg alone.

Fact.Name: Section 152(e) is satisfied by the pages of a post-1984 and pre-2009 decree
Fact.Description:
The second of the two decree routes section 152(e) admits beside Form 8332. Unlike the pre-1985 route this is not a separate statutory paragraph: IRC 152(e)(2) asks for a written declaration, and for this vintage of instrument the instructions let the DECREE ITSELF be that declaration, in place of Form 8332. So this fact is the conjunction of the vintage (../instrumentEffectiveAfter1984AndBefore2009) and the three statements the decree must make (../writablePost1984Pre2009DecreeStatesAllThreeReleaseTerms).
THE POPULATION IS REAL, unlike the pre-1985 route's, but it is NARROWER THAN THE QUALIFYING-CHILD AGE TEST and this is a rule of law, not a modelling shortfall. IRC 152(e)(1)(B) opens the special rule only for a child "in the custody of 1 or both parents for more than one-half of the calendar year", and Publication 501 reads that against state law: "If a child is emancipated under state law, the child is treated as not living with either parent", with Example 5 - a child who turned 18 in May and became emancipated - ending "The special rule for children of divorced or separated parents doesn't apply". So an 18-to-23-year-old student does NOT reach this route even with a perfect decree, and ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit is the fact that says so: not yet 18 on July 2, or permanently and totally disabled. The reachable band under an instrument that went into effect no later than 2008-12-31 is therefore a child born after 2007-07-02, plus a permanently and totally disabled child of any age. The one open residue is the age of majority itself, which this module hard-codes at 18: it is 19 in Alabama and Nebraska and 21 in Mississippi and Puerto Rico, and ../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit's own Description names those four.
THE PAGES ARE THE ATTACHMENT, which is why this route does NOT join the pre-1985 route inside ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached. IRC 152(e)(2)(B) still requires the noncustodial parent to attach the declaration, and here the declaration is the cover page, the pages carrying the three statements and the signature page. The existing intake ../writableNoncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach asks exactly that question and its Description now names the decree pages as an accepted answer, so a filer on this route who does not hold the pages is still refused - correctly.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE on both conjuncts, for the reason stated on ../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet. WHERE IT GOES: the same three places that route goes, ../parentalSomeParentNotClaiming, the noncustodial arm of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc and the custodial arm of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc - and NOT the fourth.
At least one of the parents is not claiming
True when taxpayer not filing MFJ is not claiming child
True when taxpayers filing MFJ are not claiming child

Fact.Name: In parents' custody
Fact.Description: As of July 2, was the dependent still in the legal custody of their biological or adoptive parents?

Fact.Name: Lived with taxpayer and/or other legal parent more than six months
Fact.Description: Did the dependent live with the taxpayer and/or the other legal parent for more than six months?

Fact.Name: Biological or adoptive parents living
Fact.Description: Are the dependent's biological or adoptive parents living?

Fact.Name: Nights spent with taxpayer vs. other parent
Fact.Description:
Did the dependent spend more, less, or same number of nights with taxpayer vs. other parent?
The filer is told how to count the nights: (1) A night counts for a parent when the child sleeps at that parent's home, whether or not the parent is there, or in the company of that parent away from a parent's home (for example, on vacation together). (2) The night of December 31 belongs to the year in which it begins. (3) A night the child was with neither parent (for example, at a friend's house) counts for the parent the child normally would have been with that night; if that cannot be determined, it counts for neither parent. (4) Time with a parent after the child is emancipated under state law does not count. (5) If the parents divorced or separated during the year and the child lived with both parents before the separation, count only the nights after the separation.
The night-work exception is asked separately, in ../writableNightWorkCustodialParent, because it overrides this count rather than changing how it is taken.

Fact.Name: Taxpayer's AGI higher than other parent
Fact.Description: Is the taxpayer's AGI higher than the dependent's other legal parent?
The person's parents meet the requirements of the rule for children of divorced or separated parents or parents who lived apart.

In a situation where the taxpayer is not a parent, and the person has an alive custodial parent, that custodial parent intends to claim this person as a QP for Hoh, EITC, DCC, or another credit and this person will thus not be an eligible to be the taxpayer's QP.

In a situation where the TP is not a parent, and the person has an alive custodial parent, that custodial parent is not claiming the person as a qualifying person, the taxpayer has a higher AGI than the custodial parent, which will allow the TP to claim the person for certain tax benefits.

Fact.Name: Taxpayer's situation with other legal parent
Fact.Description: The taxpayer's marital or living situation with the dependent's other legal parent, as it applies to benefit split.
Used to decide whether to display screen AddPersonParentalSupport

Fact.Name: Parental support
Fact.Description:
Did the taxpayer and/or other parent pay more than half the dependent's support?
The question counts support from both parents together, and the filer is told how to count it: (1) A PARENT'S NEW SPOUSE. When a parent has remarried, support the child received from that parent's spouse (a stepparent) counts as support from that parent. (2) ALIMONY. Alimony or separate maintenance paid to the other parent is not support of the child by the parent who paid it; count only what was spent on the child. (3) PUBLIC ASSISTANCE. Benefits the state provides to a needy person are generally support from the state, not from a parent. But TANF or similar payments a parent received and used to support the child count as that parent's support (the Publication states this rule as one made under proposed Treasury regulations).
These are counting rules for the answer, not separate questions: the answer is one yes or no for the parents together.

Fact.Name: Child's support is determined under a multiple support agreement
Fact.Description:
Is this child's support for the year determined under a multiple support agreement (a Form 2120 multiple support declaration), so that someone is treated as having provided over half of the child's support under that agreement?
When the answer is yes, the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents does not apply: the custodial parent cannot release the claim with Form 8332, and the noncustodial parent cannot claim the child through that rule. ../eligibleForBenefitSplit closes on the parental path and the child is decided under the ordinary rules.
Asked on the parental path, after ../parentalSupport. Unanswered, the benefit split is decided as if the answer were no, so silence never closes the split; an explicit no leaves it unchanged.

Fact.Name: Taxpayer is custodial parent
Fact.Description:
Is the taxpayer custodial parent of the dependent? The custodial parent is eligible to claim the person for EITC and HoH but not eligible to claim them as a dependent, or for CTC/ACTC/ODC.
The custodial parent is the parent with whom the child lived for the greater number of nights (../nightsWithTpVsOtherParent), with the higher-AGI parent on an equal count (../tpAgiHigherThanOtherParent). The night-work exception overrides that count: when, because of a parent's nighttime work schedule, the child lived more days but not more nights with that parent, that parent is the custodial parent (../writableNightWorkCustodialParent). Each override arm is fenced with IsComplete, so an unanswered night-work question, or an answer of neither, leaves the nights count to decide exactly as before.

Fact.Name: Night-work custodial parent options
Fact.Description: The vocabulary of ../writableNightWorkCustodialParent on each dependent: taxpayer (the taxpayer is the parent who works at night), otherParent (the other parent is), and neither (the exception does not apply).

Fact.Name: Night-work exception to the nights count
Fact.Description:
Because of a parent's nighttime work schedule, did the child live with that parent for a greater number of days, but not nights? If so, which parent works at night: the taxpayer, the other parent, or neither (the exception does not apply)?
When the answer names a parent, that parent is treated as the custodial parent whatever ../nightsWithTpVsOtherParent says. On a school day the child is treated as living at the primary residence registered with the school.
Asked on the parental benefit-split path, with ../nightsWithTpVsOtherParent. Unanswered, or answered neither, the nights count decides the custodial parent as before.

The person qualifies for a special benefit split, and the taxpayer can therefore qualify for either HoH, EITC, or CDCC using this person. This happens because the taxpayer is the CUSTODIAL parent and the dependency claim has moved to the other parent by one of the three routes section 152(e)(1) admits, or because the taxpayer is not a parent but is eligible for the split.
THE THREE ROUTES on the custodial side, which is what the inner Any arm holds: the taxpayer signed the written declaration themselves (../whichParentNotClaiming answers "iDid"); a qualified pre-1985 instrument gives the claim to the other parent (../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet); or the pages of a post-1984 and pre-2009 decree do (../post1984Pre2009DecreeRouteMet). On the last two the custodial parent signs nothing - the document already decided it - which is why the arm is a disjunction and not a second reading of the declaration answer. Head of household, the earned income credit and the child and dependent care credit read the qualifying child determined WITHOUT regard to section 152(e), so they stay here whichever route moved the dependency claim.
The taxpayer is the custodial parent of the dependent but says the other possible claimant signed form 8332
The taxpayer is NOT the custodial parent of the dependent but says that they (the TP) signed form 8332

Fact.Name: Form 8332 release answers contradict the custodial-parent test for this person
Fact.Description:
NO LONGER A REFUSAL TRIGGER. True when this person qualifies for the benefit split but the filer's answers about the written declaration contradict the custodial-parent test: the filer is the custodial parent on the custody test and says the OTHER parent signed the release, or the filer is not the custodial parent and says THEY signed it. The release of claim to the child (Form 8332, or a statement conforming to it) can be signed only by the custodial parent, so neither contradictory answer describes a release IRC 152(e)(2)(A) recognises.
IRC 152(e)(1) treats the child as the noncustodial parent's qualifying child only "if the requirements described in paragraph (2) or (3) are met". A release the filer describes as signed by the wrong parent meets neither: paragraph (2) fails on its own terms, and nothing in either contradiction opens paragraph (3) (the pre-1985 instrument, a different document entirely). So on the filer's own answers section 152(e) simply does not apply, and the ordinary section 152(c) tests decide who claims the child - exactly the outcome the statute already prescribes for a condition that is not met, not an unanswerable question this graph must refuse rather than guess.
WHAT HAPPENS INSTEAD, and why no other fact needs to change. On the custodial side (../contradictory8832TPIsCustodialParent) ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc's custodial arm still requires this filer's OWN signature ("iDid") or one of the two document routes; a contradictory "theyDid" satisfies none of them, so the split simply never opens for this filer and the ordinary qualifying-child tests (which do not read this Boolean) decide, with this filer as the parent the child in fact lived with. On the noncustodial side (../contradictory8832TPNotCustodialParent) ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc likewise requires the OTHER parent's signature ("theyDid") or a document route; a contradictory "iDid" satisfies none of them either, so this filer gets no claim through the special rule and the ordinary tests (which this filer will typically fail on residency, having fewer nights) decide instead. Neither fact reads this Boolean, so retiring it changes nothing else in the module.
KEPT AT A CONSTANT, not deleted, because the flow member /knockedOutByContradictory8832, the scope-sidecar knockout-guard row and the two per-side aggregator facts below all read it; no population needs the hard stop today, but the wiring stays for one that might.

Fact.Name: Contradictory release: custodial parent says the other parent signed Form 8332
Fact.Description: /knockedOutByContradictory8832 was triggered by a filer who is the custodial parent on the custody test but says the other parent signed the Form 8332 release.

Fact.Name: Contradictory release: noncustodial parent says they signed Form 8332
Fact.Description: /knockedOutByContradictory8832 was triggered by a filer who is not the custodial parent on the custody test but says they signed the Form 8332 release themselves.

Fact.Name: Knockout: the Form 8332 release answers contradict the custodial-parent test
Fact.Description: NEVER FIRES TODAY: its trigger, ../contradictory8832Knockout, is now a constant false, so this fact and its screen text below are kept only for the flow member and the aggregator facts that read them. If a future population needs a hard stop on this data-consistency pattern, this is where it is turned back on. The retired screen text, kept because it may be useful again: "Your answers about the release of claim to a child (Form 8332) contradict each other. Only the custodial parent - generally the parent the child lived with for the greater number of nights in 2025 - can sign that release. You said you are the custodial parent and the other parent signed it, or that you are not the custodial parent and you signed it. Check who the child lived with and who signed the release. This return cannot be filed here until the answers agree."
The family/household member who caused /knockedOutByContradictory8832 (the first child whose Form 8332 release answers contradict the custodial-parent test).

Fact.Name: One of the three section 152(e) routes is open on the noncustodial side, before the release-attachment answer
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer is not the custodial parent, the child otherwise meets everything the special rule requires (../eligibleForBenefitSplit), and ONE OF THE THREE ROUTES section 152(e)(1) admits is open. THIS IS NOT YET "the claim moves here" - ../whichParentNotClaiming answering "theyDid" only says the OTHER (custodial) parent signed the declaration; IRC 152(e)(2)(B) still requires THIS taxpayer to attach it, which ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc's own conjunct on ../writableNoncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach is what tests. This fact is the SCREEN GATE for that writable and for nothing else: it is what "asked when" means on that intake, kept separate so answering the release question can never make its own gate disappear.
THE THREE ROUTES, which is what the Any arm below holds. Section 152(e)(1) is satisfied when "the requirements described in paragraph (2) or (3)" are met. (1) PARAGRAPH (2), the written declaration: ../whichParentNotClaiming answers "theyDid", the other parent signed Form 8332 or a substantially similar statement. (2) PARAGRAPH (3), the qualified pre-1985 instrument: ../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet, an instrument executed before 1985 that gives the claim to the noncustodial parent, was never modified to take it back, and carries at least $600 of support. (3) THE DECREE PAGES, still paragraph (2) but with a different document: ../post1984Pre2009DecreeRouteMet, a decree that went into effect after 1984 and before 2009 and states the three things the instruction requires. An instrument that went into effect after 2008 opens neither of the last two, which is the printed bar.
THIS FACT IS A RENAME, NOT A NEW DERIVATION. Its body is byte for byte the body ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc carried before the release-attachment conjunct was added there; splitting it out kept every existing consumer of THAT fact's meaning intact while giving the screen gate a name that does not move when the release answer does.
TYPE/SIGN: Boolean, per family-and-household member, no rounding. NOT complete-safe: it inherits ../eligibleForBenefitSplit's completeness.

Fact.Name: The section 152(e) split moves this child's dependency claim and CTC/ODC to the taxpayer
Fact.Description:
The MIRROR of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc: the same IRC 152(e) split seen from the NONCUSTODIAL parent's side, gated on BOTH of IRC 152(e)(2)'s limbs: (A), tested by ../noncustodialParentSection152eRouteOpen (the custodial parent's declaration, or one of the two document routes that stand in for it), and (B), the noncustodial parent's own duty to attach the declaration, tested by the fenced conjunct below on ../writableNoncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach.
THE RELEASE CONJUNCT, and why it reads the bare Writable rather than the complete-safe ../noncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach. IRC 152(e)(1) opens only "if the requirements described in paragraph (2) or (3) are met" (26 U.S.C. 152, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section152&num=0&edition=2024). Limb (B) of paragraph (2) is a requirement, so an ANSWERED No means it fails on the filer's own answers and section 152(e) does not apply at all - the ordinary section 152(c) tests decide who claims the child instead, with no refusal. An UNANSWERED question is a different posture, a data-completeness gap rather than a failed condition, and must not silently decide the statutory question either way: the conjunct `Not(All(IsComplete(w), Not(w)))` is true whenever w is unanswered OR true, and false only when w is answered No, so only an affirmative No closes this route. THE PRE-1985 ROUTE IS EXEMPT from this conjunct by its own Any arm below: paragraph (3) carries no attachment duty at all (Form 8332 page 2 item 3b), so an instrument route filer's release answer - No, unanswered, or never asked - never closes the claim paragraph (3) already grants.
WHAT NO LONGER HOLDS: this fact is no longer byte for byte ../noncustodialParentSection152eRouteOpen (that fact is now the mirror-rename this Description used to describe); this one adds the release-attachment test IRC 152(e)(2)(B) requires. The refusal that used to fire on the whole noncustodial population reads ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached, whose residue is named there and is now narrower still: it fires only while the release question is UNANSWERED, because an answered No already closes this fact above rather than reaching that refusal.
THE THREE CARVE-OUTS DO NOT MOVE. Head of household (IRC 2(b)(1)(A)(i)), the EITC (IRC 32(c)(3)(A)) and the CDCC (IRC 21(e)(5)) each read the qualifying child determined WITHOUT regard to section 152(e), so they stay with the custodial parent. Nothing here touches a consumer of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc, which is the cheapest proof that they hold.
TYPE/SIGN: Boolean, per family-and-household member, no rounding. NOT complete-safe: it inherits ../eligibleForBenefitSplit's completeness. Its familyAndHousehold consumers (qualifyingChildUnderSection152e, qualifyingRelativeUnderSection152e) read it through a Switch: answered, it decides; unanswered while ../residencyTest is Complete true, the taxpayer is the custodial parent and the noncustodial route is not reached (false); otherwise the Switch runs off the end and the consumer stays Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Noncustodial parent has the signed release to include with the return
Fact.Description:
IRC 152(e)(2) has TWO limbs and this module modelled only the first: (A) the custodial parent signs the written declaration - which ../whichParentNotClaiming already asks - and (B) "the noncustodial parent attaches such written declaration to the noncustodial parent's return for the taxable year". This is limb (B), and it is the only thing left standing between this taxpayer and the claim section 152(e) grants them.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION - the application implements this without opening a statute.
SCREEN NAME (proposed): NoncustodialParentReleaseDocument, in the Dependents section, immediately after the existing benefit-split questions for this person and before the person's summary.
QUESTION TEXT, as asked, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "Do you have the signed Form 8332 (or a similar signed statement) from {name}'s other parent to include with your return?"
THE DECREE PAGES ARE AN ACCEPTED ANSWER on one vintage of instrument, and the screen has to say so. Where ../instrumentEffectiveAfter1984AndBefore2009 is true the question reads "Do you have the signed Form 8332 or similar statement from {name}'s other parent, OR the required pages of the divorce decree or separation agreement, to include with your return?" with the extra help text: "If the decree or separation agreement went into effect after 1984 and before 2009, you can include pages from it instead of Form 8332. You need the cover page with the other parent's Social Security number on it, the pages that say the other parent can claim {name} without any conditions, that they will not claim {name}, and which years the claim covers, and the signature page with the other parent's signature and the date. You have to include them even if you filed them with a return in an earlier year." Source: 2025 Instructions for Form 1040, "Post-1984 and pre-2009 decree or agreement", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 20, RIGHT column; Form 8332 page 2, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8332.pdf, page 2. NOT ASKED AT ALL on the pre-1985 route (../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet): Form 8332 page 2 item 3b states that route with no attachment, so ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached carries the route as a disjunct inside its Not and the refusal never reaches that population.
HELP TEXT, paraphrasing the governing instruction: "The other parent has to sign Form 8332, Release/Revocation of Release of Claim to Exemption for Child by Custodial Parent, or a statement that does the same thing, saying they will not claim {name} as a dependent for 2025. You have to include a copy with your return, and the release cannot depend on you paying support. Answer Yes only if you have that signed form or statement now." Source: 2025 Instructions for Form 1040, Children of divorced or separated parents, condition 4a - "The custodial parent signs Form 8332 or a substantially similar statement that they won't claim the child as a dependent for 2025, and the noncustodial parent includes a copy of the form or statement with their return" - https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 20, LEFT column; and IRC 152(e)(2)(B), 26 U.S.C. 152, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section152&num=0&edition=2024.
ASKED WHEN: ../noncustodialParentSection152eRouteOpen is COMPLETE TRUE for this person - that is, the taxpayer is the noncustodial parent, the child meets everything else section 152(e) requires, and the other parent signed the release (or one of the two document routes stands in for that signature). NOT ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc: that fact now reads THIS writable as its own conjunct, so gating the screen on it would hide the question the moment it is answered No - the screen gate has to be the fact as it stood before that conjunct was added. Complete true, not merely true: ../noncustodialParentSection152eRouteOpen inherits ../eligibleForBenefitSplit's completeness and is Incomplete while the benefit-split questions are unfinished, and an Incomplete gate must not open the screen. Do NOT ask it of the custodial parent (../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc) - the custodial parent signs the release, they do not attach it. Ask it ONCE PER PERSON; the household can hold more than one released child, and the answers are independent.
NOT THE FORM 8332 RENDER GATE. form8332:/writableForm8332FilesReleaseOrRevocation (form8332.xml:22) is the CUSTODIAL side - the filer who SIGNS a release or revocation and files the form itself. This writable is the other return: the noncustodial parent attaches a COPY of the form the other parent signed, and does not file Form 8332 at all. Wiring this screen to that render gate would be wrong in both directions.
UNANSWERED POSTURE, and why. Unanswered means NO. The derived ../noncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach wraps this writable in All(IsComplete(w), w), so an unanswered screen reads Complete false and /knockedOutByNonCustodialParentBenefitSplit keeps refusing exactly the filers it refuses today. That is deliberate: a return that claims a released child WITHOUT the declaration is one the IRS disallows, so the safe reading of silence is "we do not have it". There is no Placeholder and no default.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, labels "Yes" / "No", no default selection, answer required to leave the screen. No Min/Max. Nothing to normalise.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: directly, a fenced conjunct on ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc; and, through ../noncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach, ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached -> /knockedOutByNonCustodialParentBenefitSplit (flow.xml). A Yes computes the dependency claim plus CTC/ACTC/ODC through familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/qualifyingChildUnderSection152e, same as leaving the question unanswered on the pre-1985 route, which needs no attachment at all. A No CLOSES THE CLAIM RATHER THAN REFUSING IT: IRC 152(e)(2)(B) is a requirement of the special rule, so an answered No means section 152(e) does not apply on the filer's own answers, and the ordinary section 152(c) tests decide who claims the child instead - no knockout fires and no knockout copy is shown. UNANSWERED is the only posture that still refuses, through ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached: a return may not claim a released child while this question sits open.
MeF FOLLOW-ON (named, not built here): a Yes means the return carries the signed release, which MeF transmits as a binary attachment (or on paper with Form 8453). The MeF element names are not asserted here.

Fact.Name: The signed release is in hand (complete-safe)
Fact.Description: The complete-safe reading of ../writableNoncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach: All(IsComplete(w), w), so an UNANSWERED intake resolves Complete false rather than Incomplete. That matters because the refusal ../noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached negates this fact, and a knockout that went Incomplete where it used to be Complete true would change the flow on every committed scenario in this population. The IsComplete gate is on a bare Writable that is genuinely unanswered today - it is a "source answered" predicate, not a gate on a complete-safe fact.

Fact.Name: Section 152(e) moves the claim here but whether the release can be carried is still unknown
Fact.Description:
The trigger of /knockedOutByNonCustodialParentBenefitSplit, narrowed a second time. What is left is the DATA-COMPLETENESS RESIDUE and nothing else: the taxpayer to whom the split moves the claim who has not yet ANSWERED whether they hold the signed release IRC 152(e)(2)(B) requires them to attach. That residue is the correct permanent refusal for the one posture it still reaches - a return may not claim a released child while the question sits open - and it is the whole of what this guard now refuses.
AN ANSWERED NO NO LONGER REACHES THIS FACT AT ALL. The first conjunct, ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc, is itself false whenever ../writableNoncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach is answered No (its own fenced conjunct, the pre-1985 route exempt): a failed IRC 152(e)(2)(B) condition on the filer's own answers means section 152(e) does not apply, not that the return must be refused pending more paperwork. So this All is false on an answered No before its own second conjunct is even reached; only an UNANSWERED release question - where ../noncustodialParentHasReleaseToAttach is Complete false but ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc is still true - lands here.
THIS FACT'S OWN Not(...) NO LONGER DISTINGUISHES ANSWERED-NO FROM UNANSWERED: it did before the release-attachment conjunct moved onto ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc, when this fact was the only place a No or a silence was read. It is kept, unsimplified, because it is still doing one job: carving the pre-1985 route out of the unanswered-release refusal (see below), the same carve-out ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc's own Any repeats for the answered-No case.
ONE POPULATION IS CARVED OUT, and it is a NEW one rather than a narrowing of the old: the qualified pre-1985 instrument route (../qualifiedPre1985InstrumentRouteMet) has NOTHING TO ATTACH. Form 8332 page 2 sets out the two ways the condition can be met and asks for an attachment on the first only; the second is "A pre-1985 decree of divorce or separate maintenance or written separation agreement states that the noncustodial parent can claim the child as a dependent", with a support floor and no document duty. So that route is a disjunct inside the Not below and this refusal never reaches it. THE DECREE-PAGES ROUTE IS THE OPPOSITE and is deliberately NOT carved out: there the pages of the decree ARE the written declaration section 152(e)(2)(B) makes the noncustodial parent attach, so a filer on that route who does not hold them is refused exactly as a Form 8332 filer without the form is.

We should knockout the user because one they are are the noncustodial parent in a special benefit split
This does not refuse the whole IRC 152(e) noncustodial population: that population's claim now computes (../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc with familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/qualifyingChildUnderSection152e). WHAT IT NOW REFUSES is the residue named on /familyAndHousehold/*/noncustodialParentBenefitSplitReleaseNotAttached - the filer to whom the split moves the claim who has not said they hold the signed release IRC 152(e)(2)(B) requires them to attach to the return. That is a data-completeness refusal and it is permanent.
The family/household member who caused the knockedOutByNonCustodialParentBenefitSplit

Fact.Name: Eligible for benefit split
Fact.Description: Is the dependent eligible for the special rule benefit split?

On a non-parental path, the taxpayer has realized that the child qualified for the benefit split -- but that doesn't yet mean that they can claim the child.
Exported so that a consumer of ../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc can tell its non-parental arm from its custodial-parent arm: head of household and the earned income credit follow both arms, but the child and dependent care credit and the dependent care benefits exclusion follow the custodial parent alone.

The taxpayer answered questions about the person deep into the special benefit split section -- far enough that we know that the person is a QP for their parents, and that they cannot be used for tax benefits on this return.
